features.name: Controlled League data initialization and recovery

features.name: Recording Health Monitoring
features.description: Supervise every active recording with low-overhead video-frame, mux/file-growth, process, and finalization evidence so QueueBack detects a live-but-stalled or failed recorder within a bounded time, preserves later footage after recovery, and keeps a truthful actionable state in the tray and filesystem library instead of treating process liveness or parseable metadata as success.
evidence: 2026-08-12 repository inspection established that the release-era recorder proves startup mainly by child survival and does not yet provide comprehensive stalled-frame/output supervision.

2026-08-12 dependency decision: QB-PERF-002 no longer depends on this feature. Performance work may add only the minimal first-frame/progress evidence needed to prove its new capture graph, without reintroducing recording-state/library policy.
acceptance_criteria: A documented backend-neutral recording-health model distinguishes `starting`, internally `suspect`, `recording/healthy`, `recording/stalled`, `recording/recovered-after-incident`, `finalizing`, `finalized`, `finalized-degraded`, `failed-partial`, and `failed-no-output`; current health and the latched session verdict are separate so resumed progress preserves later footage without erasing a known gap.

Every production ffmpeg recording uses `-progress pipe:1`, `-stats_period 1`, and `-nostats`; stdout progress and stderr diagnostics are drained concurrently without blocking, unknown progress keys are forward-compatible, bounded parser state cannot grow per frame, and loss/malformed output cannot leave the session silently healthy forever.

Startup is not announced as healthy merely because ffmpeg is alive: within 15 seconds it must observe an advancing encoded-video `frame` counter and a positive durable `video.mp4` size, or it stops the failed startup attempt, preserves any partial bytes, persists a stable failure reason, and surfaces an actionable error.

During recording, encoded-video frame advancement and actual output-file byte growth are independent required signals; advancing audio timestamps/bytes alone cannot hide a video-frame stall, and frame advancement without durable file growth cannot hide a mux/storage stall. Output time remains diagnostic rather than sufficient health proof.

A required signal silent for five continuous seconds enters a non-user-facing suspect state; silence reaching exactly 15 seconds is a confirmed incident no later than the next one-second observation. Progress before 15 seconds returns to healthy without an incident, while progress after a confirmed incident becomes recovered-after-incident and leaves the session verdict degraded.

Any session whose required frame and file-growth signals each advance at least once in every interval shorter than 15 seconds, with valid process/observer state, cannot transition to a user-visible unhealthy state. A detected recorder scheduling/suspend gap rearms one bounded confirmation window and increments an observer-gap diagnostic instead of immediately blaming ffmpeg.

Unexpected child exit regardless of exit code, nonzero exit, stop timeout/forced kill, progress-channel closure while the child is live, counter regression, output truncation/replacement, confirmed output disappearance, repeated process-inspection failure, and terminal progress-protocol failure map to stable machine reason codes and cannot be finalized as clean success.

A confirmed stall does not automatically kill or endlessly restart a still-live ffmpeg child: QueueBack continues bounded observation so later footage can be preserved, emits transition-only warnings, and records aggregate incident count/duration/longest-stall data. Repair/remux, automatic live restart, and destructive mutation remain outside this feature.

The health reducer accepts declared required/optional signal capabilities rather than GDI, GPU vendor, or encoder names. The current backend requires encoded-frame plus output-byte progress; QB-PERF-002 can add source-frame, queue, device, and surface signals to the same model without creating a second health state machine.

Each new bundle receives an atomically written versioned `recording-state.json` before capture startup. It is the sole durable authority for recording lifecycle, current health, latched verdict, stable reason, bounded incident aggregates, last proven progress, observer gaps, and finalization result; no per-second/per-frame state-file rewrite, root status database, or duplicate health authority is introduced.

Finalization ordering is crash-conservative: persist finalizing; stop poller and ffmpeg; evaluate the structured child/progress/output result; fsync graceful clean/degraded metadata under a noncanonical pending name; atomically publish canonical `metadata.json`; then atomically persist terminal state. A metadata or terminal-state failure leaves the lifecycle authority non-success and never a clean finalized claim; the app additionally requires coherent terminal state plus canonical metadata, so forced kill, unknown exit, or unhealthy video can never be classified as clean success.

Recorder service events carry structured lifecycle/health snapshots with bundle identity and stable reason codes. Tray/headless projections show starting, recording, recovered/stalled, finalizing, and failure states; a failure or degraded terminal result is not immediately overwritten by Idle, while a later explicit new recording may replace the live tray display without erasing the prior bundle state.

The Tauri library reads the versioned state contract conservatively: a valid legacy metadata-only bundle retains its existing behavior; active/finalizing, failed, corrupt-state, and unknown-schema bundles are visibly non-complete, protected from auto-delete and active deletion, and not playback-eligible; a gracefully finalized degraded bundle is playback-eligible only under existing metadata checks and carries a clear interruption warning.

Library summaries and UI expose a typed recording status, stable problem message, physical video availability, and playback eligibility instead of calling every partial item a recovered bundle. Safe game identifiers accept the recorder's existing `digits` or `digits-suffix` collision format while continuing to reject traversal and malformed identifiers, so health state remains discoverable for every recorder-created bundle.

Live Client polling/calibration remains independent descriptive-data health: its failure never refreshes video progress, creates a video stall, or turns stalled video healthy. No active-path ffprobe, full decode, content hashing, full-file read/remux, or high-frequency frontend polling is added.

Deterministic unit and fake-child tests cover progress parsing; exact 5/15-second boundaries; startup; short-pause recovery; repeated/latched incidents; separate frame/file stalls; audio-only advancement; observer gaps; malformed/closed progress; counter/file regression; unexpected zero/nonzero exit; output missing/empty; process inspection errors; graceful stop; ignored `q`/forced kill; shutdown races; poller independence; sticky event ordering; atomic state transitions; and legacy/current/future-unknown app classification using only temporary libraries.

A real-ffmpeg changing `testsrc2` plus audio fixture proves normal startup/progress/finalization and safe forced interruption, while a 30-minute run produces zero false unhealthy transitions, bounded monitor memory/state, advancing frame and output evidence, and a truthful terminal bundle in a sentinel-marked temporary library.

A representative 25-minute-or-longer League recording verifies healthy tray state, no false alert during normal focus/Alt-Tab behavior, truthful normal finalization, app-compatible library classification, and no regression to automatic match lifecycle or Live Client synchronization. Forced interruption behavior is proved by deterministic Windows exit-probe/service tests and the real-FFmpeg forced-interruption fixture rather than a second manual League session.
